newsitem.title: BELARUS: Confusion reigns in Belarus ahead of vote.
newsitem.headline: Confusion reigns in Belarus ahead of vote.

text.p: Confusion reigned in this sleepy village outside the capital of Belarus on Saturday as voters tried to grasp a controversial referendum which has sparked a crisis in the former Soviet republic.

But fed on a daily diet of unrelenting state media propaganda for President Alexander Lukashenko's draft constitution to give him more powers, most people seemed to know whom they were voting for, if not what.

With seven questions facing her, Galina Zhuravlyova, 62, a hospital cleaner, brought a hand-written aide-memoire to polling station number 31, sat down at the voting table -- there was no private polling box -- and asked this correspondent for help.
"Can you read out the questions?" she asked.
Question one on changing the national holiday to July 3 to commemorate the liberation of the capital 20 km (12 miles) to the south from Nazi forces in 1944 was easy. She voted for it.

Number two, President Alexander Lukashenko's draft constitution on extending his term by more than two years and tightening his grip on rival institutions including a rebellious parliament, was also no problem.
"He wants to do good for people. We love him. We love him because he helps ordinary people," she said, crossing out the word "against" with zeal.
And on the "free and unlimited" buying and selling of land, which Lukashenko opposes, she was definitely against.
"Some kind of non-Russians will come from abroad and buy everything and we'll have to work like slaves," she said.
As for abolishing the death penalty, which Lukashenko also opposes, she said: "If they kill my son for nothing, or rape my daughter, why should that scum have the right to live?"
After referring again to her handwritten note, she voted against parliament's competing draft constitution which seeks to abolish the presidency in the republic of 10 million people.
"No parliament, only Lukashenko!" she declared, voting against.
But questions six and seven -- on electing local administrators instead of letting the president appoint them and on public funding -- stumped her.
Her aide-memoire told her to vote in favour, but perhaps Lukashenko wanted something else?
"What does Lukashenko want?" she asked the head of the local electoral commission, Vasily Yakushev, who was standing nearby overseeing the procedure.
"Lukashenko wants authorities to be appointed so they can work and cooperate," he replied. She changed her mind.
The last point was set by deputies who want to stop Lukashenko setting up off-budget funds without their knowledge.

"How should I vote?" she asked. "Rich people should help the authorities with money too," replied Yakushev. "But I've got written here that I should vote in favour. What does Lukashenko want?" she asked.
"He wants you to vote against," he replied. So she did.
Yakushev said people were fed up with parliament arguing with the leader, they call "batska" or father in Belarussian.
In this village 650 people of 2,412 had already cast their ballot in early voting which began on November 9, and Yakushev said he had no doubt Lukashenko's questions would win.
There were clear signs of violations. Two women members of the commission were counting unused voting papers which had no signatures or stamps as they should have.
And at another polling station on the edge of Minsk, only Lukashenko's draft constitution was pinned to the wall, while the parliamentary one was out of sight on a shelf.
Two policemen said they were on guard day and night.

"It's so much fun," said one sergeant sarcastically. "I won't vote, I can't be bothered. Why are the questions so complicated? Why can't they just say: 'Do you think criminals should be shot?' instead of asking whether the death penalty should be abolished. Whoever wrote them must have been drunk."

Even electoral commission chief Vladimir Kuzin agreed the questions were confusing. "People don't know how to vote and there are too many questions. Lots of people ask us how to answer, and we help them too," he said.
